images.title: Why multiply by three
images.purpose: Show that multiplying the top and bottom of 3/4 by 3 cuts every row of the tray into 3, turning fourths into twelfths while the amount stays the same.
images.composition: One square barfi tray on the left with plenty of space around it, and a short column of two lines of text on the right.
images.exact_structure: Left: one square barfi tray cut by solid lines into exactly 4 equal horizontal rows. Each row is split by thin grey #6B7280 lines into 3 equal pieces, making 12 equal pieces. The top 3 rows, 9 pieces, are filled teal #0072B2; the bottom row, 3 pieces, is plain. Right, top: one equation line, with both multipliers 3 drawn in reddish purple #CC79A7. Right, below it: one line naming 12. Exactly 1 tray, 4 rows, 12 equal pieces, 9 teal.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
barfi pieces that are not all exactly equal in size
images.takeaway: Multiply top and bottom by 3: same amount, new unit.
images.description: A barfi tray in 4 equal rows with 3 rows teal; each row cut into 3 makes 12 pieces with 9 teal, so 3/4 = (3×3)/(4×3) = 9/12, and 12 is a common multiple of 4 and 3.
images.context: Shown with the concept as its one key picture, next to the walkthrough video. PLACEHOLDER: specified, not generated yet.
images.teaching_notes: Ask the student to point at the teal part and say why its size did not change when each row was cut into 3.

image_decisions.why: Seeing the same teal area re-cut from fourths into twelfths explains the multiplier; one tray picture carries it.
